correctness.rationale: The orthotope facet formula and spherical-Gaussian decomposition give h_k=ER^k m_k. The half-normal cumulant κ_k is a nonzero rational polynomial in transcendental t=sqrt(2/pi) with top coefficient (-1)^(k+1)(k-1)!, for every k. Cumulant additivity, Newton identities and positive root recovery yield exact all-d inversion. Simple-root constant-term perturbation proves d−1 moments insufficient. Polynomial coefficient Lipschitz control, Rouché root matching and smooth facet-to-side inversion yield exponent 1/d; scaled simple-root perturbations around a cube prove sharpness. The bundled standalone verifier returned 844 checks including 2≤d≤8 moment inversion and 3D direct projected hull geometry; this finite test is not an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The all-dimensional minimal exact moment number, all-order half-normal-cumulant nonvanishing, and optimal inverse Hölder exponent for arbitrary orthotopes were compared by implication with three relevant historical full texts, published semantic records, and prior local claims. General projection-distribution nonuniqueness does not imply an inverse theorem for the orthotope subfamily; classical Gaussian moment identities alone do not entail the finite minimality and sharp stability assertions. Residual unindexed inverse-statistics overlap remains possible.
residual_risks: Previously unindexed shape-from-brightness statistical inversion may contain the same moment recovery or Hölder exponent.
Moment identities and Gaussian-normalization steps are standard; originality only claimed for the combined all-dimensional minimal and sharp quantitative inverse theorem.
No formal external independent novelty audit was performed.

value.rationale: The problem asks how many unlabeled isotropic shadow-volume moments are needed to reconstruct a natural d-parameter family, and how stable that reconstruction can be near the maximally symmetric cube. The result identifies the dimension-sharp minimal number, an explicit algebraic inverse, and the optimal global power of moment noise. Those are structural tomography and inverse-conditioning facts, not mere recomputation of a known single box or a trivial normalization.
